title: Asking questions to find out
keyIdea: When you do not know something, ask a person who can tell you. Need a name? Ask: what is it called? Need to do a job? Ask: how do I do it? Then listen to the answer and try it, in the same order you heard. Asking, listening and trying is how you find out.

kid: You see a bird. You do not know its name. Ask a grown-up: what is it called? Now you know. It is a robin!
You want to open a jar, but you cannot. Ask: how do I do it? A grown-up or a friend can show you.
Then listen. Mum says: hold the jar, then twist the lid. Do it the same way. Hold first. Twist next. Pop! It is open.
Ask a person who can talk back. Teddy cannot tell you, and the cat cannot tell you. Mum, Dad, Gran or a friend can.
adult: Asking to find out is one of the characteristics of effective learning in the EYFS. Development Matters (2021) asks 3 and 4 year olds to understand a question or an instruction that has two parts. The early learning goal for listening asks children to ask questions to check what they have heard. In the US, Head Start's ELOF puts asking questions and seeking new facts under initiative and curiosity.

Two kinds of information-seeking question matter most at this age: a naming question (what is it called?) and a procedural question (how do I do it?). Research on preschool questions, such as Chouinard (2007), finds that most are real requests for information, and that children who get an answer use it. The skill is the full loop: notice a gap, choose the question that fits it, pick a person who can answer, listen, then act on the answer.

Common mistakes: asking the wrong kind of question for the gap; guessing or giving up instead of asking; asking and then running off before the answer; doing the steps in a muddled order; and asking a toy or a pet. A common adult slip is to just do the job for the child. Answer the question, keep it to two short steps, and then hand the job back so they try it.

In the lab your child drags a question card to a helper to learn three names. Then they ask how to do three jobs. They hear two- and three-step answers and tap the steps in the order heard. They pick a helper who can talk back. Last, they mix it all up with new things.

familyTip: When your child points and says "What's that?", give the name and ask them to say it back. When they get stuck on a job, wait for "How do I...?" before you help. Then give two short steps, like "Push it in, then pull it up", and let them do it.

visual.caption: Which question do you ask? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: I do not know the name of a bird
I cannot open my lunch box
I do not know what this fruit is
I cannot put on my boot
I do not know the name of a truck
I cannot build my tower tall

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pick the question that fits, ask a helper who can answer, then listen and do the steps in order.

practice.prompt: You see a bird. You do not know its name. Which question helps you find out?
practice.hint: You want a name. Which question asks for a name?
practice.explain: To find out a name, ask: what is it called? A guess could be wrong.

practice.prompt: Dad tells you {n} steps. You have done 1 step. How many steps are left?
practice.hint: Take away the step you have done.
practice.explain: {n} steps take away the 1 you did leaves {=n-1} steps to do.

practice.prompt: Mum says: hold the cup, then pour. What do you do first?
practice.hint: Listen to what Mum said first.
practice.explain: Mum said hold the cup first, then pour. Do the steps in the order you hear them.

practice.prompt: You ask {a} questions in the park and {b} questions at home. How many questions did you ask?
practice.hint: Add the park questions and the home questions.
practice.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b} questions. Lots of asking means lots of finding out!

pool.prompt: You cannot zip your coat. What do you ask?
pool.hint: You know it is a coat. You need to know how.
pool.explain: You need a way to do the job, so ask: how do I zip it? Giving up means you never find out.

pool.prompt: Who can tell you the name of a flower?
pool.hint: Who can talk back to you?
pool.explain: Teddy and the flower cannot talk. A grown-up or a friend can tell you.

pool.prompt: You ask how to open a box. Gran starts to tell you. What do you do?
pool.hint: The answer helps only if you hear it.
pool.explain: Listen to Gran, then try what she says. Asking works when you listen.

pool.prompt: You learn the names of {a} birds and {b} trees. How many names did you learn?
pool.hint: Count the birds, then count on the trees.
pool.explain: {a} bird names and {b} tree names make {=a+b} new names.

pool.prompt: Dad says: push it in, then turn it. Sam turns it first. What went wrong?
choices: Sam did the steps out of order
pool.hint: What did Dad say to do first?
pool.explain: Dad said push first, then turn. Sam mixed up the order, so it did not work.

pool.prompt: You see a funny fruit. What is the best thing to do?
pool.hint: How can you find out its name?
pool.explain: Ask: what is it called? Then you learn the name of a new fruit.

pool.prompt: The grown-up tells you {n} steps to make a tower. You do them all. How many steps did you do?
pool.hint: You do every step you heard.
pool.explain: You did all {n} steps, in the order you heard them.

pool.prompt: You asked, and Mum showed you how to put on your shoe. What now?
choices: Ask Mum to do it every day
pool.hint: Asking helps you learn to do it.
pool.explain: Now you try it yourself. That is how the answer turns into something you can do.
